title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: a shape at dusk could be a post or a person, and Nyaya says that moment of not knowing is where its whole path begins

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nyaya, logic: the hetvabhasa, a reason that only looks like a reason. Which "because" did you hold up to the light? Today is our last day with Nyaya. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.
screen: `HOLD YOUR OWN UP TO THE LIGHT.` · `NYAYA, A LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: It's getting dark on a country road. Up ahead, at the edge of a field, there's a tall, thin shape standing perfectly still. Is it a wooden post? Is it a person, waiting? You slow down. You can see height. You can see it's upright. But the detail that would settle it, a hand, a face, a bit of grain in the wood, isn't there yet. For a few seconds, you simply don't know. Nyaya teachers use this very picture, the post or the person at dusk, for doubt. And they don't treat it as a failure of the mind. They treat it as a doorway.
screen: `A SHAPE AT DUSK.` → `A POST, OR A PERSON?` → `NOT KNOWING, AS A DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: The Nyaya Sutra names doubt, samshaya, among the things a seeker must understand. Doubt is a mind pulled between two possibilities, because it sees what they share and can't yet see what tells them apart. Vatsyayana, its early commentator, makes a quiet point: nobody inquires into what is completely unknown, and nobody inquires into what is already settled. Inquiry lives in between, in doubt. So the post at dusk is where reasoning starts. Look where the Sutra puts it. Its opening list of what a seeker must understand starts with the means of knowing and the things to be known, and doubt comes right after them, ahead of the example, the parts of an argument and the settled conclusion. Doubt isn't a detour on the way to reasoning. It's what gets reasoning going. And it has a shape you can work with. The post and the person share height and stillness. That's why you're stuck. So the way out isn't to stare harder at what they share. It's to look for the one mark only one of them has: a hand that moves, a bird landing on top, the grain of the wood. Nyaya trains the mind to ask, what would tell these apart? On the first Nyaya day we met the chain that runs from false knowledge to pain, and the release that comes when false knowledge goes. Doubt handled well is how one piece of false knowledge gets stopped at the door. Rush it, and you call the post a person and run, or call the person a post and walk past someone who needed help. Stay with it honestly, and one small thing gets seen as it is. For Nyaya, that small seeing belongs to the same work that ends in apavarga, release. Tomorrow we meet Nyaya's close neighbor, a school that asks a different question: not how we know, but what is there to know.
screen: `SAMSHAYA: DOUBT STARTS THE SEARCH.` · `DOUBT COMES RIGHT AFTER KNOWING.` · `LOOK FOR WHAT TELLS THEM APART.` · `APAVARGA: RELEASE.` · then, large: `WHAT WOULD TELL THESE APART?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit at dusk with one doubt. Settle, and let the breath lengthen. Bring to mind one thing you honestly don't know yet, about a person, a choice, a question bigger than both. Don't rush to decide which it is, post or person. Just stay in the not knowing, and notice what you can see: what the two possibilities share, and what detail would tell them apart. Let that be enough for now. If the mind grabs at an answer, set it down and come back to the breath. If you pray, you can hold the question before God and simply wait. The bell holds the time.
Nyaya. Today, samshaya, doubt: the mind caught between two, where honest inquiry begins, on a path that aims at release.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Today, when you meet a post-or-person moment, slow down instead of guessing. Let the doubt start an honest search. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In the Nyaya tradition, study of logic is understood as part of the path to liberation; students begin with the opening sutras of the Nyaya Sutra, which tie true knowledge to the highest good.
